This is a game of Werewolf with 5 players: 1 Seer, 1 Werewolf, 1 Possessed, and 2 Villagers. Participants: Midori, Jonathan, Mizuki, Takumi and Rin. Each player's role is secret.
- Seer: a human who divines one player each night and learns whether that player is human or a werewolf.
- Werewolf: attacks one player each night from day 1 on.
- Possessed: a human who sides with the werewolf and wins when the werewolf wins; divination shows the Possessed as human.
- Villager: a human with no special ability.

## Discussion format
The talk proceeds in days. Each day has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Jonathan, Rin, Mizuki, Midori and Takumi. On a turn, a participant either speaks, says "Skip" (passes this turn only), or says "Over" (takes no further turns this day). The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.

|---|---|---|---|---|

| 1 | the Seer is told the result of the night-0 divination (the Seer only) | 4 turns | every living player votes; the player with the most votes is executed | the Seer divines one other living player; the Werewolf attacks one other living player |

- Executed and attacked players are dead from the next day on.

## Night actions
At night, the Seer chooses one other living player to divine. From day 1 on, the werewolf chooses one other living player to attack.

## Setting
This is a game of Werewolf with 5 players: 1 Seer, 1 Werewolf, 1 Possessed, and 2 Villagers. Participants: Midori, Jonathan, Mizuki, Takumi and Rin. Each player's role is secret.

- Villager: a human with no special ability.

The talk proceeds in days. Each day has 4 turns; in each turn, every participant speaks once, in this fixed order: Jonathan, Rin, Mizuki, Midori and Takumi. An utterance is anywhere from 1 to 40 words; give it the length and content that suit the moment. An utterance consists only of the participant's own words: no name labels, headings, stage directions or commentary, and no speaking for others. The talk is a conversation among the participants: they respond to one another, asking, answering, agreeing and objecting, and the decision grows out of that exchange.
